trail: Usually a bounding trail of several animals that have run, skidded and jumped together, so individual details are hard to read; hind feet land ahead of the front feet and usually do not register on top of them, and when bounding the two front feet land one behind the other. Tail drag marks are sometimes visible.
dung: Dark brown tubes 6-8 mm in diameter, surprisingly large for the animal, packed with insect fragments. Latrines sit on the eastern side of termite mounds where the group basks in the morning sun, especially in winter.
signs: Small diggings a few centimetres across where insects were dug out, often alongside the tracks
Excavated termite emergence holes with discarded alate wings scattered around
Latrines on the eastern edge of occupied termite mounds
High-pitched hissed alarm calls from sentries and faint hissing or whistling contact calls
Yellow-billed hornbills gathered on a termite mound at dawn betray a resident group
facts: Track lengths measured at Londolozi: front 31 mm, hind 25 mm; Africa's smallest carnivore
The group changes den almost every night, so tracks lead between termite mounds
Diminutive size plus evidence of long claws is the key to identifying this track

why.paraxerus-cepapi: Same bounding gait and size, but the squirrel's front feet land side by side or overlapping (mongoose front feet one behind the other), the squirrel usually shows five hind toes with the three middle ones bunched tightly, a square tread-patterned main pad and shorter claws.
why.mungos-mungo: Banded mongoose track is larger (front 39 mm vs 31 mm) and its droppings are much larger (about 12 mm vs 6-8 mm).
why.rodent: Dwarf mongoose tracks are so small they are often taken for a rodent's; look for the four long claw marks.

track: A small track with four clearly showing oval toes and sharp claw marks that register in almost any substrate. Front toes are more splayed; hind toes are bunched more closely, and the hind first toe sits so high on the foot that it never prints and its claw only rarely does. The rear edge of the front main pad is asymmetrical, one lobe extending lower than the other. The front proximal pad, first toe and claw appear occasionally, but not when the animal is moving fast.
trail: In a normal walk the hind foot lands in front of, or occasionally on top of, the front foot. At speed it bounds, leaving a pattern like a hare's: two hind feet side by side ahead of the front feet, which land one behind the other.
dung: Dark brown to almost black, one or two thin cylindrical tubes 7-11 mm in diameter and 30-40 mm long, with insect remains.
signs: Tracks follow road edges, open clearings and game paths through long grass or thick vegetation
Tracks in mud at the edges of waterholes and small pans, which it visits regularly
Climbs trees when hunting or disturbed
Dives into adjacent cover when startled
facts: Track lengths measured at Londolozi: front 36 mm, hind 28 mm
Diurnal but stays in cover in cold cloudy weather; solitary or in pairs
Characteristically travels along the edges of roads and clearings

why.genetta-tigrina: Genet has a much larger main pad, round rather than oval toes, and seldom shows claws unless moving fast.
why.genetta-genetta: Genet has a much larger main pad, round rather than oval toes, and seldom shows claws unless moving fast.
why.paraxerus-cepapi: Squirrel shows five hind toes with the three middle ones grouped tightly and a differently shaped main pad; mongoose toes are more evenly spaced (see tree squirrel sheet, p225).
why.mungos-mungo: Banded mongoose track is about 14 mm larger (front 50 mm with proximal pad vs 36 mm).

track: A large mongoose track with long, broad, widely splayed toes typical of a wetland animal, yet no webbing between them, and short thick claws sitting close to the toe tips. Front toes splay more than hind toes. Five toes on each foot, but the first toe and its claw are not always clear, and the proximal pad prints only when the animal moves very slowly on soft ground, in which case the front first toe and claw do show. Without first toe and proximal pad the front print (46 mm) looks shorter than the hind (52 mm). The rear edge of the front main pad has two distinct outer lobes, the outer one extending much lower than the inner one, giving it a lopsided form.
trail: The usual gait puts the hind foot on top of the front foot, though several gaits are used. Trails run long distances up and down river banks, even where little water is visible.
dung: Latrines near the water's edge; droppings 50-100 mm long and about 20 mm in diameter, smaller than the Cape clawless otter's, containing crab carapaces, hair and fragments of small aquatic animals. Unlike otters it leaves crab shells only partly broken up.
signs: Latrines on rocks and banks beside rivers, dams and swamps
Crab fragments scattered along river edges where it fed
Resting places in grass patches and on floating vegetation
Tracks in mud along water margins
facts: Track lengths measured at Samara Game Reserve: front 46 mm, hind 52 mm (without first toe and proximal pad); drawings 70 mm front and 62 mm hind with them
Occurs in large numbers at Samara in the semi-arid Karoo, far from obvious water
Nocturnal and crepuscular; solitary, in mating pairs, or a female with young

why.ichneumia-albicauda: White-tailed mongoose has shorter toes set more tightly together, longer claws, and its large first toe and claw do not show in the track.
why.aonyx-capensis: Otter droppings are larger and the crab carapaces in them are completely demolished, while water mongoose droppings (about 20 mm wide) hold recognisable shell pieces.

track: Five toes on each foot but normally only four register; the first toe is seldom seen, although the claw of the front first toe can leave a mark in mud or soft fine soil. The four toes sit in a semicircular arc with the two middle toes close together, most tightly on the hind foot. Long, obvious claws print on both feet. The front main pad has an asymmetrical rear edge, its outer lobe reaching lower than the inner; the hind main pad is roughly square along its leading edge.
trail: In the walking sequence the hind foot lands ahead of or over the front foot. Now and then the hind claws are dragged very lightly across the ground.
dung: Droppings 12-16mm in diameter, holding insect fragments, fruit and even leaves (buffalo thorn berries and leaves recorded); left in latrines as well as scattered at random through the territory.
signs: Latrines with fruit- and insect-filled droppings, often with Ziziphus mucronata berry remains
Diggings made with the strong front claws for burrowing insects, beetles and larvae
Occupies termite-mound holes dug by aardvark and other animals rather than digging its own
Anal-gland scent marks on territory; known to raid chicken runs
facts: Measured at Londolozi Game Reserve: front 52mm, hind 51mm, nearly equal in length.
Nocturnal and mostly solitary; long legs and a bright white bushy tail.

why.lupulella-mesomelas: Jackal toes are much larger and its front and hind tracks run roughly 5-8mm longer; jackal middle and outer toes lie in parallel pairs and its main pad has a symmetrical rear edge, whereas the mongoose toes form an arc and its pad rear is slightly asymmetrical.
why.atilax-paludinosus: The water mongoose has shorter claws and longer, more widely splayed toes, and its big first toe and claw often show, which they never do in the white-tailed track.

track: Five large, round-tipped toes on both feet that usually mark clearly, with no claw marks at all (only three hind toes carry small claws, and these do not print). The hind foot is larger than the front, with bigger, more splayed toes; the webbing is not visible in the track. A big main pad shows, and a proximal pad behind it in soft ground, though the proximal pad is often indistinct; the full outline of the foot rarely prints.
trail: At a walk the hind foot lands on top of the front or just beside it. The faster lope gives a 1-2-1 pattern: front, then a half-registered front/hind pair, then hind; a side lope with the body turned leaves a diagonal row of four prints repeated each stride. Otters cover long distances, often following dry riverbeds between water sources.
dung: Droppings 22-28mm in diameter and 30-50mm long, made mostly of crab-shell fragments, deposited in latrines on open ground; also small 'spraint' deposits of fish scales and bones bound in black jelly-like anal-gland secretion.
signs: Latrines on open ground near water with shell-filled droppings
Fragmented crab or mussel shells and fish scales left on the bank where prey was eaten
Burrows in river banks under dense vegetation or rocks close to the water's edge
Scent marks from a pair of glands under the tail
facts: Measured at Londolozi: front 110mm, hind 118mm; the hind foot is the larger, built for swimming.
Most active early morning and late afternoon; solitary or in small family groups.

why.atilax-paludinosus: A water mongoose feeding in the same spot confuses the picture, but the mongoose usually leaves larger shell fragments than the otter.
why.panthera-pardus: In riverbeds where prints are blurred, the clawless five-toed otter track with its big main pad is sometimes taken for a leopard, especially by trackers expecting leopard there.
why.chlorocebus-pygerythrus: When all five long toes print clearly the otter track can look like a vervet monkey's.

track: Five large oval, sausage-shaped toes on each foot, although the first toe and its claw sometimes fail to print. Front claws are exceptionally long (25-30mm); the middle three usually show clearly and can strike up to 20mm ahead of the toes, while hind claws are much shorter. On the hind foot the three middle toes sit so close together they often look fused. The main pad is large and unsegmented, with a single proximal pad set to the outside behind it, half-moon shaped on the hind foot and hard to make out on hard ground.
trail: Hind foot lands behind the front foot, sometimes at a slight angle, occasionally on top of it; at a faster walk the hind lands ahead of the front. Front feet often point slightly inwards (pigeon-toed) while hind feet face the line of travel or turn outwards. Tracks of a pair are not unusual.
dung: Dark, coarse droppings 15-20mm in diameter and 60-80mm long, containing hair, feathers, insect remains and seeds.
signs: Deep excavations dug with the front claws for hibernating snakes (puff adder), scorpions, dung-beetle larvae, mice, bulbs and lizards
Dug-up mocca bee (Trigona) hives with comb and larvae scattered on the ground
Will climb trees to scavenge a leopard's kill
Generally diurnal but turns nocturnal where it feels threatened
facts: Measured at Londolozi: hind foot 80-93mm long, main pad 50mm wide; front foot 108-112mm including claws (drawings 110mm front, 85mm hind).
Front claws alone reach 25-30mm and can print up to 20mm ahead of the toes.
Front feet turn in, hind feet straight or out: a useful cue for which foot is which.

why.hystrix-africaeaustralis: Porcupine toes are smaller, rounder and more splayed (front usually four toes, hind sometimes five) with short stubby claws, a main pad split into three by faint ridges, usually two proximal pads, a 70-80mm track against the badger's 80-110mm, hind on top of or just behind the front, and sometimes quill drag marks.
why.panthera-pardus: In unclear substrate the badger's big unsegmented main pad can suggest leopard, but the long claw marks and five sausage-shaped toes separate it.

track: Front foot has four toes and is about 37 mm long; the larger hind foot has three distinct toes and is about 48 mm. The giveaway is the long main sole pad: the soles are big, soft, rubbery and segmented (kept moist by glandular secretions for grip on rock), and in soft ground the segmentation of the front main pad shows. Front feet are plantigrade (flat-footed), hind feet semi-digitigrade. The hind inner toe carries a grooming claw that may or may not print; hind tracks usually register more clearly than fronts.
trail: Bounding gait like a hare or other rodent-type hopper, with hind feet landing ahead of the fronts. Look on roads and paths right next to rocky outcrops and koppies.
dung: Pellets 7-10 mm in diameter, dark brown, easily taken for a small antelope's. Deposited in communal latrines that can grow very large, with white streaks of crystallised calcium carbonate from the urine on the rock beside them.
signs: Latrines on and below rock ledges with white crystallised urine stains running down the rock face
Dorsal scent gland (patch of long black hair mid-back) used for social and territorial marking
Sentries on vantage points giving sharp bark alarm calls; at least 20 distinct vocal signals
Bark stripped from branches of trees they climb; browsing on buffalo thorn and Combretum leaves
Natural rock crevices used as dens; they do not dig
facts: Three toes behind, four in front: an odd combination for a mammal this size
Crepuscular; feeds twice a day in bouts of under 30 minutes and lives in herds of 10-80
Crystallised hyrax urine is sold at muti markets in Johannesburg and Durban as a stomach remedy

track: Human-like tracks, especially the hind foot with its characteristic big toe. Both feet have five digits with an opposable thumb or big toe; the hand's thumb stands off from the index finger and often does not print. The hind foot (142-155 mm at Londolozi) is twice the length of the front (70-80 mm) with a broad, rounded heel, and the large round joint of the big toe between the main pad and the toe itself is diagnostic. The front foot is short with long, thick, parallel digits held tightly together and short nails; in soft ground the fingerprint creases show.
trail: Normal walk is an understep: the hind foot registers just behind the front foot of the same side. Baboons walk flat-footed and leave tail drag marks only where they sit.
dung: Lumpy droppings 30-50 mm in diameter, light or dark brown to dark green, texture coarse-grainy to fine depending on diet.
signs: Extensive shallow diggings over large areas for roots, bulbs and insects, with logs and rocks turned over and vegetation stripped
Loud barking alarm calls, mainly for lion and leopard, given from treetops while staring at the threat (easily confused with troop squabbles)
Roosts in tall evergreen trees or secluded rocky outcrops at night
Remains of hunted small mammals such as impala fawns in the lambing season
facts: Measurements from Londolozi: front 70-80 mm, hind 142-155 mm, varying with age
Hind foot is double the length of the hand, with a broad rounded heel
Tail drag only appears where the baboon has sat down

why.potamochoerus-larvatus: Baboon soil diggings look like bushpig rootings but are shallower.
why.chlorocebus-pygerythrus: Baboon hind heel is broad and rounded while the vervet's is narrow and pointed (V-shaped); an adult baboon hind foot is 40-50 mm longer; baboon hand digits lie tight and parallel whereas vervet digits splay; vervets grip the soil leaving little mounds of sand and often drag their tails, baboons walk flat-footed; young baboon tracks can be confused with adult monkey tracks.

track: Small primate hand and foot, five digits each with an opposable thumb or big toe; the hand's thumb sits at just under 70 degrees to the other digits. Digits are long with short nails that rarely print. Front digits (55-70 mm foot) are longer and splay more than the hind, especially at speed; hind digits (80-93 mm foot) are shorter and bunched together, splaying only when the monkey hurries or turns. The hind heel is a relatively narrow, pointed V, unlike a baboon of similar size.
trail: Walking, the hind foot is placed next to the front foot. Tail drag marks are common from both walking and sitting, and the varied movement and gait make the trail very hard to follow.
dung: Cylindrical droppings from very short to quite long, 15-25 mm in diameter and 50-100 mm long; dark green to brown depending on diet, darkening with age, often with berries, seeds and insect fragments.
signs: Little mounds of soil raised at the base of the digits where the monkey grips the ground
Tail drag lines between tracks
Distinct alarm calls for leopard, snake and eagle, given while staring at the predator
Retires to trees at night; troops of up to 40 with a clear dominance order
facts: Londolozi measurements: front 55-70 mm, hind 80-93 mm, depending on age
Hand thumb set at just under 70 degrees to the fingers
Measurements and drawings show great variation in the length and shape of monkey tracks

why.papio-ursinus: Vervet tracks are easily confused with a young baboon's: monkey digits splay more often, the baboon heel is wider and bolder, and the monkey leaves little soil mounds at the base of its digits whereas the baboon walks flat-footed.

track: Tiny five-digit prints, rarely found. The hind track is 25-30 mm long with an unusually large opposable big toe set well apart from the other four toes, which prints clearly; the front foot (about 20 mm) is of similar length but seldom shows unless the animal is moving slowly on all fours. Digits, palms and soles are cushioned with subcutaneous tissue for travelling through thorny branches.
trail: On the ground the lesser bushbaby hops bipedally on its hind feet, so the left and right hind tracks register close beside each other with no front prints; quadrupedal movement is rare.
dung: Unsegmented, irregular, elongated droppings about 5 mm in diameter and 15 mm long, light to dark brown, usually with visible insect fragments.
signs: Scent marks of chest-gland secretion and urine rubbed onto hands and feet and deposited on branches along the route
Males urinate on females to mark them
Feeding on gum of Senegalia and Vachellia (acacia) trees, especially in winter
Loud chattering alarm call, plaintive defensive call and a territorial call
Communal daytime rest in tree holes or dense foliage
facts: Weighs about 150 g and leaps 3-5 m between branches; far more arboreal than the thick-tailed bushbaby
Hind track 25-30 mm, front about 20 mm, but tracks are rarely seen
Takes all its water from food

why.chlorocebus-pygerythrus: Can be confused with a young vervet monkey (no separating criterion given on the sheet).
why.otolemur-crassicaudatus: Thick-tailed bushbaby tracks are up to 30 mm larger and usually show both front and hind feet, whereas the lesser mostly leaves only hind prints.

track: Thick hair under the feet and between the toes blurs almost everything, so the print is usually a soft smudge with no clear toes, claws or main pad. In mud the four toes, claw tips and single pad sink in and show, and the print can then pass for a small jackal. Hind foot (37 mm) is slightly larger and longer than the front (30 mm); when the hare sits up on its hocks the two hind prints lengthen and imprint in full. Claws only register when it accelerates or turns sharply.
trail: Classic hare bound: one front foot down, the other directly ahead of it, then both hind feet swing around and land side by side a few centimetres apart, ahead of the fronts. Bound length grows with speed.
dung: Pale green to yellow oval pellets about 12 mm long, left in small heaps; marginally bigger than Cape hare pellets. A second, dark mucus-coated caecal pellet is re-ingested straight from the anus and is seldom found.
signs: Lies up in a 'form', a shallow natural depression under long grass or a small bush, which may keep the body impression in the soil
Does not normally use other animals' burrows or holes
Grazes short green grass, turning to leaves, rhizomes, roots and small shrub stems when grass is scarce
facts: Nocturnal but also out in early morning and late afternoon; mostly solitary, though several males trail a female in oestrus and groups gather on good grazing
Prefers open savanna woodland with grass and scrub

why.Cape hare: Nearly identical, but the scrub hare hind print is marginally smaller; where both occur (Karoo) the scrub hare keeps to denser scrub and the Cape hare to more open ground.
why.sylvicapra-grimmia: A single smudged hare print can be mistaken for a small antelope print such as a duiker's; look for the bounding group of four and the absence of a cleft hoof.
why.lupulella-mesomelas: In mud, where toes, claws and pad show, the hare print resembles a jackal's; the hare's trail pattern (paired hind prints ahead of the fronts) gives it away.

track: Four toes on every foot, but usually only three long toes with long thick claws imprint clearly, so the track looks like a fork pressed into the soil; on perfect substrate all four toes and claws show. The main pad is often indistinct, though the hind foot has a noticeably larger, extended main pad. Front about 40 mm, hind about 50 mm.
trail: Walks along habitual routes; the book gives no gait pattern, only that tracks are found on its regular runs.
dung: Dark brown pellets about 20 mm long with a characteristic groove running along the length of each pellet.
signs: Well-worn paths or 'runs' 80-100 mm wide through grassy areas and vleis, used regularly
Little piles of cut, discarded grass or reed stems where it has been feeding
Teeth-chattering sound while cutting grass with the upper incisors
Grass nests above ground or shallow burrows in marshy areas and along river and lake banks
Grunts or hisses when alarmed and bolts for water or thicket
facts: Heavily built rodent of up to 10 kg, nocturnal, living in small groups led by one male
Regarded as a pest in sugar cane plantations; preyed on by leopards and smaller carnivores in the Sabi Sands

why.mungos-mungo: Both leave similarly sized long claw marks, but the banded mongoose shows four clearly marked toes and claws where the cane rat regularly shows only three.

track: A strange print to match the animal: the main pad is split into three segments by faint ridges, and two further proximal pads sit directly behind it; spotting these two proximal pads is the key to the track. Both feet carry five toes but usually only four round toes with short stubby claws register, the first toe often missing; toes are more splayed than a honey badger's and very indistinct in loose sand. Track length 70-80 mm (drawings: front 80 mm, hind 76 mm), measured at Samara in the Karoo and Londolozi near southern Kruger; some individuals have unusually long front claws.
trail: At a normal walk the hind foot registers on top of, or just behind, the front foot. Dragging quill marks often run alongside the prints.
dung: Black droppings 16-23 mm in diameter, either small round pellets or longer cylinders, often clumped and strung together, full of root and bark fibre. Dropped at random, occasionally in a midden.
signs: Shed quills lying about; a scatter of quills over a small area marks a confrontation
Narrow diggings for bulbs and roots, with the eaten root exposed at the bottom of the hole
Bark stripped from the lower trunk of trees such as tamboti (Spirostachys africana)
Bones and bone fragments carried into burrows (osteophagia)
Scent marks rubbed with the anal gland on rocks, the ground and small plants, sometimes with quill marks below the rock
Occupies burrows taken over from aardvarks, also rock crevices and caves
facts: Africa's largest rodent; mainly nocturnal, monogamous, and may travel very long distances in a night's foraging
Comparison table: honey badger five toes always show, porcupine front usually four and hind occasionally five
When threatened it raises its quills and reverses into the attacker, leaving quills behind

why.mellivora-capensis: Honey badger prints are larger (80-110 mm vs 70-80 mm) with big oval sausage-shaped toes, the three middle toes bunched tightly (especially on the hind foot), very long thick front claws, one unsegmented main pad and a single proximal pad; the porcupine has smaller rounder evenly spread toes, short claws, a three-segment main pad and usually two proximal pads, and its hind foot lands on top of the front whereas the badger's lands behind.
